1:
The heading and the occasion are settled first. Delitzsch names this the opening of the Hodu-psalms, those beginning with the call to give thanks, as distinct from the Hallelujah-psalms, and reports that the festival song David handed to Asaph at the setting down of the Ark draws its first part from this psalm before continuing with another and closing with a third. He notes that Hitzig reverses the dependence, taking the chronicler's version for the original and the psalms for shoots off it. Clarke and Calvin both accept David's hand in the substance while judging the whole to have been enlarged later, probably at the restoration from Babylon; Calvin adds that it has no title in the Hebrew or Chaldee, the Hallelujah closing the previous psalm having been carried over as an inscription by the ancient versions. Augustine begins from that borrowed word, since this is the first psalm to which it is prefixed, and takes the confession commanded here to mean praise rather than acknowledgment of sin, as when the Lord confessed to the Father.

What the opening summons asks for is read at two levels. Gill treats the call as addressed to the whole congregation and turns each verb inward: confess the Lord's greatness, confess him as Creator and covenant Father, and confess also your own sins and unworthiness. Henry enumerates seven duties in the four verses and supplies a reason for each, insisting that praying for further mercy is itself accepted as acknowledgment of mercy received, and that God's wondrous works belong in ordinary family talk and not only in worship. Spurgeon presses the missionary edge: make known his deeds among the nations, that the heathen may forsake their idols, and take care that singing is unto him and not for the music's sake. Calvin narrows the subject deliberately. The psalm does not celebrate the government of the world, as the preceding one did; the wonders meant are not the sun and the seasons and the provision made for every living creature, but the free adoption of one people out of the ruin of Adam's race, so that the language is addressed to believers only.

The strength to be sought divides the commentators. Gill takes it for the ark, called the strength of God because his power had been shown by it at Jordan and Jericho, and a type of Christ; he notes a rendering that makes it seek the Lord in his strength, and another that the versions give as seek the Lord and be strengthened. Wesley agrees that it means the ark, and glosses the face as the gracious presence. Ellicott rejects the whole line: the verb is better rendered enquire after, the congregation is being pointed toward the historical survey that follows, and the strength must therefore mean the manifestation of divine power in the deeds about to be recited. Clarke, characteristically, keeps it devotional and personal, making the face reconciliation and the seeking a man's chief business.

The closing arguments are agreed. Henry finds them in what God has said and done, in the relation the hearers stand in as the seed of Abraham born in his house and therefore bound to a servant's duty, and in their interest in him. Gill hears the name Jehovah as self-existence itself, incommunicable to any creature, and yet the God of the covenant. Clarke says the same more briefly and refers the reader forward, remarking that the historical abstract which follows presents few difficulties. Wesley takes the judgments in all the earth for God's executions upon all nations, and Ellicott notes that the opening verse stands word for word in the prophets and was apparently one of the recognized doxologies of the Hebrew Church.
8:
Henry takes the whole section as an instruction in how to praise: look a great way back, and give God the glory of what he did for the church when it was being founded, since later ages enjoy the benefit. He notes that the parallel passage in the chronicler turns the same fact into a duty, and calls it a covenant rather than a promise because something was required on man's part. Spurgeon presses the same point harder: the exhortation to remember gains its force from the fact that God has remembered first, and never once in any instance has he been unmindful of his engagements. He notes that the promise is said to be commanded, and so carries the authority of a law that will stand though heaven and earth pass away. Wesley glosses the remembering as remembering so as to perform, and Ellicott prefers appointed or conferred to commanded.

The ratifications are counted out. Henry lists them as an oath, a law and an everlasting covenant, so that the thing is made sure by everything that can make anything sure, and observes that the three men named are grandfather, father and son, all eminent believers. Gill reads the word law as bearing on God rather than on men: the covenant is not of the nature of the old covenant of works, but has the force of law with respect to God himself, who by condescending grace has laid himself under obligation. Ellicott, more soberly, says the two Hebrew words for law and covenant appear here to be used as synonyms, and elsewhere notes that the ordinary verb for making a covenant is to cut one. Spurgeon supplies the scene, the divided victims and the burning lamp passing between the pieces. Gill and Henry both make the land a type, Gill drawing the parallel at length, a land of promise answering to the promised inheritance, prepared and furnished, entered only through many battles; Ellicott says only that the verse marks the scope of the psalm, to show how the promise to Abraham was fulfilled.

The patriarchs' smallness is the hinge of the next argument. Delitzsch renders the phrase as men of number, men easily counted, and notes that the following verb sets their dependence on one people's hospitality after another in a relation of cause and effect. Gill draws the moral that Canaan was granted for neither their numbers nor their goodness, and applies it to the little flock. Henry works the exposure into three heads: they were few, they were strangers and so likelier to be abused and less able to help themselves, and they were unsettled, driven from nation to nation by famine. Clarke adds only that all appearances were against them.

The protection is read as the more remarkable for that exposure. Gill instances Isaac and the herdsmen of Gerar, Laban restrained from hurting Jacob, and the terror of God falling on the cities round about, and adds that the world's enmity to the seed of the woman is rooted but not permitted. Ellicott points instead to the incidents concerning Sarah and Rebekah at the courts of Egypt and Philistia. Henry makes the point that even crowned heads were checked, Pharaoh plagued and Abimelech rebuked, and draws out that God's anointed prophets are dearer to him than anointed kings. On who the anointed are, Wesley names the three patriarchs and explains the title from their consecration and their prophetic converse with God; Ellicott concedes the term is not technical here, since they were never actually anointed as later prophets and kings were, but defends it from its application to the covenant people as a whole; Clarke widens it further, suggesting the whole nation may be meant, a kingdom of priests. Gill takes it of all believers, anointed with the oil of grace.
16:
The famine is read as an act of command. Gill notes that the calling brought it, famine being a servant at God's order, and Ellicott gathers the parallels treating famine, war and pestilence as emissaries to be summoned and sent. Spurgeon presses the broken staff: as a cripple falls when his staff snaps, so does man when bread fails; and he adds that God had wise ends in it, the scarcity being his method of leading his people down into Egypt. Henry adds that all judgments are at God's call and no place exempt when they are sent with commission, and that the staff was broken even in the land of promise so the patriarchs might see God designed them a better country.

Joseph's descent divides on almost nothing. Gill and Ellicott both anchor the sending in Joseph's own account of providence in his life, Gill adding that God is said to send him although his brethren sold him. Henry asks in what character the man went who was to prepare a reception for the church, and answers that he went neither as ambassador nor as agent but as a slave for life, then lower still as a prisoner falsely charged. Gill adds that the fetters were heavy enough to gall him, which the history omits but he takes as certain. On the clause about the iron, Ellicott is unusually candid: the syntax rather favours the Prayer Book reading that the iron entered into his soul, the gender of the verb favours the margin, the ancient versions divide, and the parallelism supports the received text.

The release turns on what word came. Gill offers the interpretation given to the butler and baker, the report of it reaching Pharaoh, or the divine word about Joseph's exaltation. Clarke distinguishes the clauses, referring the first to the prison dreams and the second to Pharaoh's, called the oracle of the Lord because sent by him. Ellicott sharpens the second verb: better purified than tried, God proving Joseph innocent of the charge by enabling him to foretell the dreams. Wesley agrees, the word purging him of the calamities cast upon him. Henry turns it into a rule: there is a set time when God's word will come for the comfort of those who trust it. On the exaltation Gill catalogues the offices and makes each a figure of Christ, lord of the house that is the church; Henry does the same at greater length and adds that Joseph was made great in order to do good, especially to the household of faith.

The multiplying in Egypt and the change of heart close the section. Gill notes that sixty-six went down and six hundred thousand came out, the people increasing the more they were afflicted. Spurgeon turns that into the proverb that the more they were oppressed the more they multiplied, and adds that it is idle to contend with God or his people. Henry observes that the church, like the believer, flourishes most while under persecution. Delitzsch puts the mechanism plainly: the oppression was God's work only indirectly, in that he gave his people a might which excited Egyptian jealousy, and the craft reached its pitch in the attempt to weaken them by killing the children. The hardening is handled carefully by everyone. Gill denies that God put any hatred into the Egyptians, since human hearts need no such supply, saying only that he did not restrain it and did the things which occasioned it. Wesley compresses this to a word, that God suffered their heart to be turned. Clarke prefers the passive rendering of the versions and explains the change politically, as curtailment once the Hebrews grew too strong. Ellicott notes that the hardening of Pharaoh is ascribed to God throughout the narrative. Spurgeon offers the analogy of the sun, which softens wax and hardens clay and is blamed for neither.
26:
The signs are described before they are listed. Gill notes that the Hebrew reads the words of his signs, and that the ancient versions turn the phrase round so that God put those words into Moses and Aaron, one rendering it into both and another as he did his signs by them. Ellicott offers the alternative that the construction means the details of his signs, signs in sequence, sign after sign. On Moses himself Gill makes the servant a type of Christ, sent to redeem from a worse than Egyptian bondage.

The darkness carries the chapter's hardest crux. Ellicott states it squarely: the list omits the fifth and sixth plagues and opens with the ninth, and the appended clause about not rebelling has troubled translators from the first. Of the Egyptians it is plainly untrue, and referring it to Moses and Aaron he calls feeble; the Greek and Syriac cut the knot by dropping the negative; reading the verb as a purpose clause, that they might not rebel, leaves the ninth plague's position unexplained. He therefore prefers a proposed emendation which by a slight change yields that God darkened them so they might not discern his tokens, making the plague a figure of the moral blindness the Egyptians showed throughout. Clarke reaches for the same kind of remedy, suggesting a letter lost from the front of the verb so that it reads they did not observe his word, and offering as his other option that Moses and Aaron are meant, since the Egyptians rebelled throughout. Wesley takes that second option without argument.

Through the plagues themselves Gill keeps two registers at once. He numbers each in its Exodus order, the blood first, the frogs second, the flies fourth, the hail seventh, the locusts eighth and the firstborn last, silently correcting the psalm's own sequence; and he reads each as a type of the vials poured on spiritual Egypt, blood given to the antichristian states for having shed the blood of the saints. He canvasses the mixture of flies, which some take for wild beasts and the versions for dogflies, and defends the verb killed as applied to vines and fig trees, since classical writers speak the same way of inanimate things. Clarke notes that the smiting of the vines is not in Exodus at all. Ellicott observes that the psalmist has added a second insect to the locust named in the history, a poetical synonym for the parallelism, whose root means licker.

The march out draws the warmest writing. Gill defends the spoiling of the Egyptians as equitable payment for unpaid labour and insists the verbs mean asked and gave, against those who make it unwilling on either side. Ellicott and Wesley both press the word for feeble: not one stumbler, none unfit for the march, which Wesley calls wonderful in a body so vast and so long oppressed. On the cloud Gill raises a real difficulty, that the pillar stood upright and went before them rather than covering them, and canvasses the answers that it sheltered them at rest but not on the march, or that there were several clouds; Ellicott says frankly that the reason given in the histories has been lost sight of and the pillar has become a canopy against the sun; Spurgeon exults, asking what travellers in the desert would give for such a covering, and adding that the psalm selects the happier theme and dwells only on covenant love, though the tale of Israel's sin is as extraordinary. Both Spurgeon and Wesley notice that the quails were granted despite the sin of the asking. Clarke ends with a specimen: a fragment of the rock at Horeb lies on his desk, fine granite with felspar, mica and quartz distinct, and since granite is reckoned the basis of the earth he makes it the one remaining emblem of Christ in creation.
